Date: 14-May-26
Reference Number: 20016785
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architect
Purpose: Safeguarding Digital Sovereignty When Using American SaaS Solutions in Defence
Question Asked: Our defence organization is considering the use of SaaS-based IT service management solutions such as ServiceNow, an American provider. We are seeking guidance on how to safeguard digital sovereignty and data security, particularly regarding sensitive CMDB registrations. Can Gartner assist in identifying best practices, risk mitigation measures, and key considerations to maintain sovereignty and compliance when hosting critical IT processes in the cloud, specifically within the context of defence requirements and evolving international regulations?
Analyst Name: Robert Stoneman
Discussion Summary: Sovereignty Overview:

Gartner defines digital sovereignty as an organization’s ambition to maintain control over its data, operations, and technology in the face of external influences, ensuring continued innovation and resilience. Fundamentally, the use of any foreign supplier within any element of your technology stack and its supply chain, will theoretically limit your sovereignty to some extent. Therefore, it is important to consider that sovereignty is not binary: it is a spectrum, with most organizations opting to settle on a degree of sovereignty depending on their needs. 

However, governments often concentrate digital sovereignty on data residency and cloud service localization. While important, this narrow focus risks overlooking deeper dependencies that can compromise mission resilience and public service continuity. Digital sovereignty encompasses more than where data is stored — it includes who controls the infrastructure, platforms, and applications that underpin public-sector operations. 

Gartner considers three critical types of sovereignty risks: 

•	Data sovereignty: “I need to have authority over the location of and access to my data.”

•	Operations sovereignty: “I need authority over how my environment is operated and by whom.”

•	Technology sovereignty: “I need to have full authority over my technology stacks, including physical infrastructure, and be able to run them in a disconnected manner, possibly.”

In terms of how this breaks down in terms of cloud deployment options, Gartner maps these three sovereignty levels across the following options: 

 

Bear this in mind considering the trade-off between sovereignty levels and cost/scalability/functionality. 

For more information, please see the following research note: 

Prioritize on Sovereign Capabilities When Choosing Your Cloud Provider 
Geopolitical uncertainty and the sovereignty requirements of applications, operations, and infrastructure in global public cloud environments have led to several sovereign cloud offerings. Executive leaders can use this research to map public cloud provider approaches to their sovereignty requirements. 
Published: 15 Sep 2025 
Rene Buest | Gregor Petri 


ServiceNow and Sovereignty:

Considering a U.S. vendor like ServiceNow, there will always be limits as to which types of sovereignty risks can be addressed. ServiceNow has a range of deployment options (this is based on my broad knowledge of the platform…I would strongly recommend following this up with one of our analysts who specialises in this vendor). Please see below for a recent snapshot of this: 

 

Its SaaS-based offerings (on the left) will at best provide you data sovereignty (e.g. via encryption of your data) and partial operational sovereignty (e.g. due to its Sovereign Cloud offering using isolated clouds that theoretically should help protect against the risk of service cut-off). Also bear in mind its Sovereign Cloud offering is currently only available in the U.S., Australia and Singapore to the best of my knowledge. 

Even though its customer/partner offerings go further (e.g. due to its Private Stack being a customer/partner-operated deployment model), it would still not provide full technology sovereignty unless you were able to operate it for the medium-term with no support or patching from ServiceNow. However, of the available deployment options, this would be best suited.

Also, bear in mind that while “Private Stack customers receive the same application software as cloud customers”..., “some features [are] unavailable due to dependencies on ServiceNow-hosted services.” According to ServiceNow, this is the rough breakdown of features available:

•	Available
o	Now Assist 
o	AI Agents & Knowledge Graph (Zurich+)
o	AI Search & Predictive Intelligence
o	RPA, Process Mining, Automation Center 
o	Security Incident Response & Threat Intelligence
o	Field

Analyst Name: Nic Breidel
Discussion Summary: How Sheriff’s Stations Are Using CRMs
1. Citizen Request and Case Management

Centralized Intake: CRMs provide a single portal for citizens to submit non-emergency requests, complaints, or inquiries (e.g., noise complaints, lost property, community concerns).
Automated Routing: Requests are automatically assigned to the appropriate divisions or deputies, ensuring timely follow-up and resolution.
Transparency: Citizens can track the status of their requests, increasing trust and accountability.

2. Community Engagement and Outreach

Event Management: CRMs help organize community events, safety workshops, and outreach programs, tracking attendance and feedback.
Targeted Communication: Sheriff’s offices use CRMs to segment audiences (e.g., neighborhood watch groups, business owners) and send targeted alerts or educational materials.

3. Victim and Witness Support

Case Follow-Up: CRMs facilitate ongoing communication with victims and witnesses, providing updates on investigations, court dates, and available support services.
Resource Coordination: Integration with social services or victim advocacy groups ensures individuals receive timely assistance.

4. Internal Workflow Automation

Incident Tracking: CRMs can log internal incidents (e.g., use-of-force reports, equipment requests) and automate approval workflows, reducing administrative burden.
Performance Analytics: Dashboards track response times, case closure rates, and community satisfaction, supporting data-driven decision-making.

5. Records and Evidence Management (Integration)

While not a full replacement for dedicated records management systems (RMS), CRMs often integrate with RMS and CAD (Computer-Aided Dispatch) systems to provide a holistic view of cases and interactions.

6. Compliance and Reporting

Audit Trails: CRMs document all interactions and actions taken, supporting compliance with state and federal regulations (e.g., CJIS requirements).
Custom Reporting: Automated generation of reports for internal review, grant applications, or public transparency initiatives.


Industry Examples and Research

Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department: Uses CRM-like platforms to manage public records requests, community feedback, and track non-emergency service requests.
Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office: Implemented CRM to streamline communication with the public and automate case management workflows.
Industry Research: According to a 2023 Center for Digital Government survey, over 60% of sheriff’s offices and police departments are exploring or have implemented CRM solutions for improved constituent engagement and operational efficiency.


Key Benefits

Improved Responsiveness: Automation reduces response times and ensures no request falls through the cracks.
Enhanced Public Trust: Transparency and proactive communication foster stronger community relationships.
Operational Efficiency: Streamlined workflows free up deputies for core law enforcement duties.


Considerations for Implementation

Data Security: Ensure the CRM is compliant with CJIS and other law enforcement data standards.
Integration: Select platforms that integrate with existing RMS, CAD, and evidence management systems.
Change Management: Invest in training and stakeholder engagement to drive adoption.


Summary:
Sheriff’s stations are leveraging CRMs to bridge the gap between law enforcement and the community, automate administrative processes, and enhance service delivery. The right CRM, such as ServiceNow or a similarly robust platform, can deliver measurable improvements in efficiency, transparency, and public satisfaction.

This situation is becoming increasingly difficult with SAP unable to demonstrate value from SAP AI for customized ERP landscapes, and using an evolving policy to prohibit or make it difficult for customers to extract their own data to apply non-SAP solutions that could.
This comes as at time when AI is struggling to show any ROI, Gen AI [such as SAP Joule] being a poor match for ERP use cases [better served by numerical AI variants].  All ERP vendors face this AI challenge with GenAI offering little value other than as a digital assistant to help information retrieval or when used as a conversational user interface.  ERP is being better served by non GenAI technologies such as simulation, optimization and rule based logic.

This limited access for large organizations with few large projects using SAP AI which today lacks any significant case studies

Core customizations block or restrict benefits so standard features or agents (designed to work with standard business processes and workflows) delivers limited value. SAP Custom Agentic AI part of SAP Joule Studio, but these solutions are not exclusive and available to all organizations including on-premises.

This policy was followed with SAP’s announcement to offer their new SAP Business AI Platform services to all customer including those with on-premises landscapes.

Date: 11-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20060453
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Quality Management
Purpose: Interaction Follow up (Ref # 20029223)
Question Asked: Hello Tyler, 

Thank you for your reply. I have further enquires. 
1.	Change control ensures every change is assessed for risks and impact before implementation. It was mentioned that there is a need to define what constitutes a change in a cloud context. Can you share examples of how it is being defined by other organizations? What are the examples where change control is not required (unlike that for traditional ITSM) to prevent bottlenecks? For context, there is no CAB approval required. However, all changes are to be approved by 2 levels of line managers prior change deployment. 
2.	As organisation adopts self-healing systems or AI-driven remediation, how do we continue to meet the same change control objectives?
3.	In SaaS environments (e.g. Salesforce, ServiceNow), how do we continue to meet the same change control objectives?
4.	From Gartner’s experience, how do mature organisations use platforms such as ServiceNow and Jira/JSM together to govern requirement and change requests
Analyst Name: Tyler Cheney
Discussion Summary: Hello Ivy,

Thank you for your follow-up regarding cloud change practices.  I’ve done my best to answer your questions below, but please feel free to reach out with any questions.

1.  I think fewer and fewer orgs are treating every cloud action as a change in the traditional sense.  Typically, they distinguish between changes to infrastructure-as-code (e.g., a pull request to change how Terraform provisions resources) and runtime changes (someone manually reconfiguring a host in the console).  The former goes through a peer review and pipeline-based approval process.  The latter is either blocked outright via policy-as-code or at least flagged for review.
In terms of where change control isn't required to prevent bottlenecks, the most common exemptions are auto-scaling events, certificate renewals handled by automation, patching managed by the cloud provider, and config changes made by approved automation pipelines with adequate testing.  The principle behind all of these is the same: if the change is automated, bounded in scope, reversible, and was authorized when the automation was configured, creating a standard change is sufficient.  Standard changes are pre-approved and serve as a means to log changes without adding to the bottleneck.

2.  In theory, things should get much easier as AI and automation maturity increases, as long as you continue to create more standard changes and log them automatically pre-change.  When you create an automation to handle a change workflow, the building of that automation goes through the normal change process.  When it is needed in production, standard changes are created to log the actions of the automation.  What the automation does at 2am is then just execution of an already-approved automated workflow.
The change control you’re replacing with standardized changes (authorization, traceability, risk assessment, rollback capability) are still satisfied with automated resolution.  Authorization happens at with the original RFC to build the automation.  Traceability comes from automation execution logs and automatically-logged standard changes.  Impact assessment is baked into the scope you determined before building.  Rollback capability needs to be tested upfront as part of approving the resolution logic in the first place.  If any of those four aren't covered, the automation isn't ready to run unsupervised.

3.  Typically, this is handled by tracking release schedules (both Salesforce and ServiceNow publish these well in advance), testing changes in a non-prod instance, and documenting tests per your requirements.  The testing record is the evidence of control, even though you didn't initiate the change.  A change should be created on your side to document when it occurred and to attach the test results.
The part that gets overlooked is post-change configurations.  Someone with admin access trying to get a service back online could make a quick field change in production without going through the change process.  The only real way to solve that problem is stronger access controls.

4.  Typically, JSM owns the delivery lifecycle (i.e., user stories, epics, bugs, sprint planning) and ServiceNow owns the operational governance side (i.e., changes, incidents, problems, CMDB).  The integration happens when a new build/release needs to be promoted from development to production.  Meaning, a Jira ticket triggers a ServiceNow change when the work is ready to deploy.  The change record in ServiceNow captures the authorization, the deployment window, the risk assessment, and the post-change review.  The Jira ticket captures the requirements, design decisions, and test evidence.  Together they give you a traceable thread from business requirement through to deployed change.
The integration doesn't have to be technically complex.  A lot of orgs just require a ServiceNow change number to be referenced in the Jira ticket before a deploy

Date: 10-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20071918
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Services
Buyer Role: Head of Infrastructure and/or IT Operations
Purpose: ITSM Chatbot Development (Copilot-ServiceNow Integration)
Question Asked: Grant Nicholas is interested in developing an ITSM chatbot using Copilot and ServiceNow to improve responsiveness and utilize their knowledge base effectively. He seeks to understand how Copilot can be integrated with ServiceNow to create a more flexible and efficient chatbot solution. Questions are - How can we integrate Copilot with ServiceNow to develop an ITSM chatbot? What are the best practices for storing knowledge base articles, and should they be stored in SharePoint or ServiceNow? Can Copilot agents be set up to process data from Sentinel SIEM?
Analyst Name: Tyler Cheney
Discussion Summary: Hello Grant,

Thank you for your inquiry regarding chatbots. I’ve done my best to answer your questions below, but please feel free to reach out with any questions.
On the core integration question, Copilot Studio is where you build the chatbot, then connect it to ServiceNow via Power Automate (or Power Apps) flows or direct REST API calls using ServiceNow's Table API or Scripted REST APIs.  What this gives you over native ServiceNow Virtual Agent is flexibility in the conversation model and workflow.  You're not locked into ServiceNow's topic-based decision tree structure, which sounds like exactly what burned you last time.  ServiceNow Virtual Agent (without the NowAssist AI add-on) requires you to define conversation topics, pre-build conversational flows, and hand-code fallback responses, which is too rigid compared to a GenAI-based chatbot.  Copilot Studio lets you lean on a GenAI layer that can handle open-ended phrasing and pull context from connected knowledge sources rather than matching user input to a predefined path.  That's the biggest difference in practice, especially for an ITSM environment focused on end-users, where users can phrase the same request a dozen different ways.
For the actual ITSM actions, you'd connect Power Automate to ServiceNow to handle things like incident creation, ticket status lookups, password resets, or CI queries.  The chatbot captures the user intent, Copilot Studio orchestrates the logic, and the Power Automate flow handles the low-level actions.  It works reliably for well-scoped actions and gets messier the more complex the ServiceNow data model gets, so start with your highest-volume, lowest-complexity request or incidents categories and build out from there.
On where to store knowledge base articles, the honest answer is that it depends on who owns the content and how it gets updated.  SharePoint integrates natively with Copilot Studio through the built-in knowledge source connector, so if your KB articles live in SharePoint, the bot can search with semantic search without you building anything custom.  ServiceNow’s Knowledge Base is the better home if your articles are tightly coupled to your ITSM workflows, linked to CIs or problem records, or need to follow an approval and lifecycle process (and you don’t already have a tool capable of that).  However, the two aren't mutually exclusive.  A reasonable approach is keeping operational, process-driven KB articles in ServiceNow where they belong, and maintaining broader IT guidance or how-to (self-help) content in SharePoint where Copilot can reach it more easily.  The risk with splitting them is content drift, where the same information lives in two places and gets out of sync, so you need someone accountable for that.  If your team already struggles with KB hygiene, consolidating to one location and accepting the integration tradeoffs is probably the right way to go.
Regarding Copilot agents and Sentinel, yes, this is doable, but it needs to be designed.  Microsoft Copilot for Security has native Sentinel integration, and a Copilot chatbot can pull from Sentinel datavia the MS Security Graph API or Power Automate with the Sentinel connector.  Where this gets complicated is around access control.  Sentinel data is usually sensitive, and you need to make sure the agent's identity only has read-only access unless it specifically needs write access.  One thing worth noting is that pulling raw Sentinel data into a chat interface is useful for L1 triage, but it can also generate noise if the agent pulls everything indiscriminately.  Think about what questions the user is actually asking before you design what the agent returns.
Data sovereignty is certainly worth being specific about.  Copilot (and the broader MS Power Platform) operate within your MS365 tenancy, and your data residency follows your tenant's geographic region settings.  Data processed through Azure via Copilot i

8. **Integrate Multi-Agent Environments**
   - Implement multi-agent environments to manage and streamline GRC processes.

9. **Promote Role Evolution and Task Breakdown**
   - Break down and clearly define tasks to reduce concerns about job displacement due to automation, emphasizing the importance of human decision-making.

10. **Unify GRC, Third-Party Risk, and Privacy Management**
    - Consolidate cyber GRC, third-party risk management, and privacy processes onto a single platform for improved oversight and efficiency.

11. **Consider Establishing a Risk Operations Center**
    - Evaluate the establishment of a risk operations center to oversee integrations and leverage wide coding for easier process integration.

12. **Engage Team in Change Management**
    - Involve the GRC team in redefining job roles and responsibilities post-implementation to ensure adaptability and comfort with new tools and processes.

13. **Provide Ongoing Support and Research**
    - Offer continuous access to research, training, and support resources to facilitate a smooth transition and maintain stakeholder satisfaction.

These insights guide the successful implementation of ServiceNow IRM and AI, while ensuring GRC security analyst roles evolve to meet new organizational needs.

- Saikat Ray outlined key use cases for agents, such as knowledge assistance, processing unstructured data, and case management, where agents enhance decision-making rather than replace human judgment.
- Chris described their current approach of using agents to assist underwriters by performing preliminary checks on unstructured data, while keeping humans in the decision-making loop.
- Saikat Ray identified three types of vendors in the agentic solutions market: package vendors, open platforms, and hyperscalers, noting a trend towards more packaged solutions.
- AWS was highlighted as a potentially enterprise-ready platform due to its governance features, while other platforms like ServiceNow and Microsoft were also mentioned for their strides in AI management.
- The discussion touched on the evolving nature of the market, with Saikat Ray expressing caution about the maturity and production readiness of certain open-solutions like n8n.
- Chris expressed concern about the rapid evolution of the space and the need for reliable governance and security in financial services, indicating a preference for established platforms like AWS.
- Saikat Ray shared insights on the limited production use of platforms like OpenAI and Cloud for enterprise-grade applications, suggesting packaged platforms or hyperscalers as more viable options.
- The conversation concluded with an acknowledgment of the hype versus the actual adoption rate of agentic solutions, which remains low due to unresolved governance and security challenges.

Date: 7-May-26
Reference Number: 20029223
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Quality Management
Purpose: On-premise Change Management Workflow
Question Asked: HDB has both on-premises application systems and cloud products.  The ServiceNow workflow currently covers enhancements to on-premises systems only. 

Cloud product teams follow 3 loops namely-Discovery, Delivery and Operation- where Discovery activities are  managed outside SHIP-HATs (e.g. email,  spreadsheets), and Delivery and Operation activities are managed in SHIP-HATs.  No ServiceNow integration for cloud products has been defined at this stage.   

When should requests or information transition between ServiceNow and SHIPHATs for cloud products?

How can duplication or inconsistency be avoided across the two platforms?
Analyst Name: Tyler Cheney
Discussion Summary: Hello Ivy,

Thank you for your inquiry regarding Change across the two environments. I’ve done my best to answer your questions below, but please feel free to reach out for anything else:
The on-premises Change Management workflow is applicable to cloud products at its core, but it needs adjustment to fit how cloud delivery actually works.  The fundamentals are the same, like having a formal record of what's changing, who approved it, what the risk assessment is, and what the rollback plan is.  The main changes are the pace (much faster in the cloud typically) and the way changes are initiated and executed (automation).  On-prem changes tend to assume longer lead times, manual deployment steps, and a relatively low frequency.  Cloud product teams can deploy multiple times a week or day, changes tend to be smaller and more incremental, and deployment is typically automated through pipelines.  So, if you apply an on-prem workflow directly to a cloud product team without modification, you'll either slow them down or they'll work around the process entirely.  The adjustments you need should be tailored to your product teams pipelines, but there are general best practices around change categorization, approvals, and how standard changes are defined.  Routine, low-risk cloud deployments that go through a well-known pipeline should be classifiable as standard changes with little-to-no CAB review required.  Formal review should be for significant changes, where the success of the change isn’t guaranteed, where post-deployment outcomes are unknown, anything with significant production risk.

The governance changes that come with extending this to cloud products are mostly about acknowledging that cloud delivery operates differently and building that into your process and CAB structure.  Meaning, define what constitutes a change in a cloud context, since not everything that gets deployed is necessarily a change in the traditional ITSM sense.  A config flag toggle in a feature management tool or replacing a container usually aren’t considered CAB-worthy.  You draw those lines clearly by creating as many known, standard changes as possible.  Anything else will be slowed down by the bottleneck of review and approval.  You also need to decide who owns change approval for cloud products.  Cloud teams often sit closer to the product than to traditional IT operations, and the CAB composition may need to reflect that.  If your current CAB is entirely infrastructure and operations-focused, cloud product leads probably need a seat at the table, or you need a lightweight review mechanism that's calibrated to their usual risk level.

The main difficulties organizations run into when trying to standardize across both environments usually come down to three things: process, tooling, and culture.  On process, the same change management procedure applied uniformly to both environments tends to either be too rigid for cloud or too loose for on-prem.  Teams end up either gaming the classification system to avoid overhead, or the process becomes a rubber stamp that adds no real governance value.  On tooling, on-prem workflows tend to be well-supported in platforms like ServiceNow, but cloud delivery pipelines live in separate tools, and without integration, you end up with the duplication problem you already described.  Integrating the two worlds together should actually reduce duplication and ensure that records are synced and contain links to records from other platforms.  This keeps a historical record chain in place.  On culture, cloud product teams often come from a DevOps background where the philosophy is that process overhead is a bottleneck.  Getting those teams to engage seriously with a change management process requires that the process demonstrably not get in their way for routine work, or you'll lose the battle regardless of what the policy document says.  This is where you fight fire

Date: 17-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19470524
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Energy and Utilities
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architecture - Other Role
Purpose: WR: Knowledge Management Platform Comparison
Question Asked: What are the main strengths and weaknesses of ServiceNow Knowledge Management (KM)  compared to BloomFire and Shelf?
What are the most common selection criteria for ServiceNow KM, and how does client adoption compare to the other vendors?
Can you provide a summary table of pros, cons, and core capabilities for all three platforms?
Analyst Name: Darin Stewart
Discussion Summary: Hello Pablo Bisceglia,





Thank your question regarding knowledge management platforms. ServiceNow Knowledge Management (KM), Bloomfire, and Shelf are all very capable enterprise knowledge management platforms, but they each take a very different approach and serve different audiences.. ServiceNow KM is a very ITSM focused module inside the broader ServiceNow platform. Bloomfire is a knowledge engagement / enterprise intelligence hub targeted at backoffice knowledge workers. Shelf is a GenAI-first KM platform  optimized for contact centers and operational teams and more recently providing semantic integration across knowledge stores and business applications.

ServiceNow is without question the market leader in KM for ITSM and helpdesk/contact centers, but ONLY as an element within such an environment that has adopted the larger ServiceNow platform. Also, non-ITSM and contact agent users generally do not like interacting with the platform. It has advanced AI capabilities, strong security, and flexible workflows. It can also identify potential knowledge gaps in its knowledge bases.  If you are currently a ServiceNow user and the target user-audience is mainly ITSM or Contact / Help agents,  ServiceNow is an excellent choice, otherwise probably not.

Bloomfire is, in many ways, the opposite of ServiceNow KM.  It is designed as a centralized knowledge hub to collect, share, and grow internal knowledge across teams, with deep integrations with other enterprise platforms.  In contrast to ServiceNow, Bloomfire has a very intuitive, user experience which simplifies onboarding and adoption.  Its search capabilities are outstanding as are its content authoring and management capabilities. The downside is that it is whole unsuited for ITSM situations or contact centers that require ticketing or incident tracking. Bloomfire focusses on decision support when knowledge is centralized and easily discoverable. It is a good fit for organizations wanting to use KM as a strategic intelligence layer rather than for ITSM and ticket tracking and call deflection.


Shelf is sort of a middle ground between ServiceNow and Bloomfire.  Is is a GenAI forward knowledge management platform, with strong abilities facilitated with Search Copilot and GenAI Content Copilot that assist contact agents by suggesting the right knowledge asset in the current context. It also supports multilingual content and decision tree support.  More recently, Shelf has introduced strong content processing and integration capabilities to semantically reconcile content and knowledge from different source systems. Despite this, Shelf is not a full enterprise workflow platform. You'll still need ITSM, CRM, HR systems, etc., and integrate Shelf as a knowledge layer. It is a good alternative to ServiceNow if you already have ITSM and Ticketing systems that are not ServiceNow.

As requested, below is a comparison table.  I hope this is helpful.  Please let me know if I can be of further assistance.

-dls-


Dimension
ServiceNow Knowledge Management
Bloomfire
Shelf
Primary Positioning
ITSM-/Service workflow–embedded KM for IT, HR, CSM, and other service teams.
Enterprise knowledge engagement / intelligence hub for CX, sales, marketing, and cross-functional teams.
GenAI-first KM platform optimized for contact centers and operations (Search Copilot, Content Copilot).

Date: 3-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19445942
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Healthcare
Buyer Role: Divisional Technology Leader
Purpose: ServiceNow Observability Capabilities
Question Asked: The client has requested a written response to clarify how ServiceNow’s observability‑adjacent capabilities are distinct from, yet complementary to, observability platforms. The goal is to provide clear guidance on how these capabilities are positioned within an enterprise operations architecture.
Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: Hi Joe,

This is the written response I said I would provide when we chatted last week. My intent is to clearly explain the differences and architectural interdependence between a dedicated observability platform, such as Grafana Cloud, and the Service Observability capabilities built on ServiceNow ITOM. Confusion between these offerings can arise because both environments work with operational signals and both contribute to improved reliability. The remainder of this note explains how the types of signals involved and the roles they play in the architecture differ, and how those differences are intended to be complementary.

ServiceNow does ingest and process operational data. Through ITOM, AIOps, and Health Log Analytics, it consumes events, metrics, and logs that are relevant to operational decision‑making. In practice, these inputs are typically selected, filtered, aggregated, or correlated to represent conditions that are meaningful in a service or operational context. Common examples include alerts raised by monitoring or observability tools, events derived from metric thresholds or anomalies, health indicators calculated across components, correlated event streams, and log patterns identified as operationally significant.

These signals are normalized, associated with services and configuration items via the CMDB, and enriched with ownership, dependency, and change context. They are then evaluated to support prioritization, escalation, and response. The objective is to answer operational questions such as which business service is affected, how severe the impact is, who owns remediation, and what workflow should be triggered. Architecturally, this positions ServiceNow as a system of action, coordination, and governance.

This differs from what we refer to as cross‑telemetry analysis. Cross‑telemetry analysis operates closer to the telemetry emitted by systems themselves and is focused on understanding system behavior, rather than immediately driving operational workflows. At this stage, the data being ingested is not limited to alerts or service health summaries, but consists of the underlying telemetry that describes how applications and infrastructure are actually behaving. Examples include high‑cardinality metrics, distributed traces, application and platform logs, and resource usage profiles. These telemetry types capture rich behavioral detail, such as request latency distributions, error characteristics, request‑level context, and resource consumption patterns. Once telemetry has been reduced to events or health indicators, many cross‑domain relationships are no longer observable.

In observability platforms such as Grafana Cloud, these telemetry types are retained and queried together, enabling relationships to be explored across domains. Engineers can correlate a latency increase in a service metric with specific trace paths, related log patterns, and resource saturation on downstream components. Analytical features help surface anomalies and potential correlations, while still allowing engineers to interactively explore and validate findings. For example, a spike in request latency may appear in ServiceNow as a service health degradation, while in Grafana Cloud it can be analyzed in context with specific trace paths, log messages, and backend resource behavior to determine the underlying cause. The value at this layer is explaining why a system behaves a certain way and identifying emerging or previously unknown issues.

A practical distinction worth making explicit is distributed tracing. Dedicated observability platforms ingest and analyze full‑fidelity traces and spans as first‑class telemetry, enabling reconstruction of end‑to‑end request paths and correlation with metrics, logs, and infrastructure behavior. ServiceNow does not function as a native distributed tracing platform. While trace identifiers or trace‑derived events can be ingested and
================================================================================

- The framework was broken down into four areas: Plan, Track, Optimize, and Empower, with each area focusing on different aspects of cost management and accountability.
- In the 'Plan' phase, Ang suggested ensuring basic FinOps training for those creating financial liabilities and setting standards for cloud application design and deployment.

- In the 'Optimize' phase, Ang discussed right-sizing, scheduling, and using spot instances to reduce costs, while also addressing the need for centralized management of commitments like reserved instances.
- Ang advised against starting with modernizing architecture due to the need for broader buy-in and maturity, suggesting it as a later step in the FinOps journey.
- The 'Empower' phase focused on building accountability through showback and chargeback mechanisms, and Ang highlighted the importance of providing actionable insights to stakeholders.
- Ang emphasized the need for tracking remediation actions in a structured way, integrating them into existing systems like Jira or ServiceNow for better management and accountability.

What is Gartner's position on tools like Lumos compared to established players like SailPoint and Saviynt? How can we find a tool that is more economical yet effective for our needs? What are the potential risks and benefits of choosing a newer player like Lumos over traditional leaders?
Analyst Name: Scott Brinker
Discussion Summary: Summary/Ask:

The Sonoco team is looking at options to find a cost-effective solution that offers robust capabilities without the high costs associated with established players like SailPoint and Saviynt
In 2023, Sunoco identified a need for an IGA capability and initially pursued Pathlock, which was unsuccessful but need to re-evaluate other potential vendors such as Lumos
They have concerns about trying another vendor due to past challenges and potential for buy-out or acquisition

Key Takeaways:

Gartner classifies vendors like SailPoint, Saviynt, and Omada as full-featured, cloud-architected SaaS-delivered IGA solutions
Full-featured solutions are designed to manage comprehensive identity governance across complex hybrid architectures
They are the preferred choice when organizations require advanced governance functions like role-based access control (RBAC), automated role modeling, dynamic segregation of duties (SOD) controls, and intricate compliance policy enforcement
Gartner classifies Lumos as a "IGA light tool“ focusing on speed and simplicity
Lumos is designed to unify identity governance, just-in-time access management, and life cycle orchestration into a single solution
Lumos has a strong emphasis on visibility, AI-driven automation (via its "Albus" multiagent system), and managing cloud and SaaS environments
Consider an IGA light solution if your governance demands are straightforward and you do not require heavy customization
Evaluate your exact needs – if your needs do not extend significantly beyond manual access reviews, and you do not need to build and maintain complex
IGA light tools can be augmented with other tools third-party specialized tools (like risk analytics, role-mining tools, or specific SCIM gateways) to address specific functionality gaps 
IGA light solutions are quick to deploy, easier to maintain and have good visibility and intelligence such as AI
IGA light solutions may not integrate well with legacy systems and may lack advanced governance features as well as limited customization/certification functions
Consider existing tools such as ServiceNow, MS Entra, Okta

Date: 22-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19482848
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: Software Engineering - Other Role
Purpose: Observability Strategy
Question Asked: As the client modernizes platforms and integration architecture, they need to ensure observability supports reliability, operational efficiency, and business insight across multiple layers and personas.
Key questions:

Are we designing observability correctly across foundational platforms, integration layers, and delivery teams?
How should open telemetry, tagging, labeling, and log ingestion be implemented to ensure reuse and consistency?
How can technical observability effectively roll up to business and executive-level visibility?
Are skill gaps or operating practices contributing to current observability challenges?
Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: These are the key takeaways I sent to the client after the call:

Establish platform observability as the foundation. Ensure Kafka (e.g., brokers, Connect, consumer lag), Kubernetes, and core integration services are reliably observable before optimizing downstream consumers or business use cases.
Use native integrations and OpenTelemetry (OTel) for technical health and add custom instrumentation when business context is required. Technical observability can mostly rely on out-of-the-box signals, but business and transactional observability require deliberate metadata added in your OTel instrumentation.
Do not make dashboards the center of your observability strategy. Dashboards should support situational awareness and investigation, while alerts, notifications, and guided queries handle day-to-day operations.
Progress deliberately from reactive to proactive observability. Start with clear rules and thresholds, evolve to anomaly detection once signals stabilize, and treat predictive capabilities as an advanced stage rather than a starting point.
Templatize dashboards and instrumentation to reduce manual platform effort. The platform team should own standards and templates, while service teams adopt them rather than requesting bespoke builds.
Capture only essential, non-PII metadata to enable business observability safely. Focus on low-cardinality identifiers such as internal transaction or correlation IDs, and avoid payload data that increases cost, risk, or latency.
Design explicitly for asynchronous and decoupled architectures. Correlating events across Kafka, retries, delays, and SaaS boundaries is an architectural decision that must be addressed intentionally, not assumed to come from tooling.
Rely on alerts and incident workflows as the operational backbone. Use Grafana detections to trigger ServiceNow incidents with clear routing, severity, and ownership rather than depending on customer-reported issues.
Use absence-of-signal as a first-class detection pattern. Proactively detect silent failures, such as consumers not consuming or expected events not occurring, rather than focusing only on explicit error signals.
View AI as a digital teammate that amplifies good instrumentation, not a replacement for it. AI-driven insights only deliver value once telemetry is consistent, well-structured, and aligned to how the platform and business actually operate.

Date: 17-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20080445
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Energy and Utilities
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architect
Purpose: Insights on Save Your Failing CMDB With a Service Data Model
Question Asked: what major pitfalls or gotchas has gartner seen when producing the research called 'Save Your Failing CMDB With a Service Data Model'
Analyst Name: Tyler Cheney
Discussion Summary: Hello Amitabh,

Thank you for your inquiry regarding our CSDM research!  I’ve done my best to provide more insight below, but please feel free to reach out with any questions.
The single most common mistake is treating CSDM as just another project instead of the foundational element that will be used to suppor their IT operations.  Teams spend months populating CI classes and mapping relationships before they've agreed on what use cases the CMDB actually answers.  CSDM gives you a framework for how to model your environment, but it doesn't tell you why you're modeling it or what decisions will be driven by that data.  If nobody has defined the use cases upfront (impact analysis, change risk assessment, cost allocation, etc), you end up with a beautifully structured CMDB that nobody queries because it doesn't map to how the business does its work.
Related to that is scope creep.  The CSDM entities (Service Instance, Tech Mgmt Offering, Business Offering, etc.) are useful, but orgs frequently try to populate all of them at once, with complete data and relationship information, before governance is put into place.  The result is a half-built model that's already drifting from reality before it goes live.  The better approach is to pick one entity where you have reasonable source data and actual downstream consumers, prove the value there, then expand.  Trying to boil the ocean with CSDM is how you get an overly-long implementation with no value.
Another one that catches people off guard is ownership.  CSDM pushes you toward explicit ownership of services.  Very quickly, orgs discover they don't actually have clear service owners, or the people in those roles don't know they're supposed to be maintaining CMDB data.  Without that accountability integrated into your platform, the model starts degrading almost immediately after go-live.  Discovery tools can help with the technical data, but they don't know your application portfolio or your service definitions, so the upper layers of CSDM require human maintenance.
The integration assumptions are also a recurring problem.  CSDM works best when it's the authoritative source that other tools consume, but most orgs already have a sprawl of products with their own data models baked in.  Getting those to align with what you've built in CSDM is a hefty effort, and it's always underestimated.  People assume the CMDB will become the system of record by virtue of existing, but it doesn't work that way.  You have to actively route processes through it and deprecate the competing models, which is political as much as it is technical.
Finally, there's the ServiceNow-specific reality that CSDM is a moving target.  ServiceNow has revised the model across multiple releases, and if you're not on a recent version or haven't kept up with the changes, your implementation may not align with current best practices or product features that depend on specific CSDM constructs.  Some of the newer ServiceNow capabilities assume a reasonably current CSDM implementation.  Worth checking where your version lands before you commit to a design.

Analyst Name: Ashish Banerjee
Discussion Summary: Key ask:
To determine whether Navy Air can adopt a cloud-based ITSM platform by implementing a tiered CMDB and layered controls to meet regulatory and security requirements.

Summary:
- Ashish Banerjee framed the discussion around Navy Air’s ITSM hosting, emphasizing regulated critical infrastructure and strict data boundaries.
- He cautioned against viewing the decision as simply cloud risk versus no cloud risk, highlighting operational maturity and execution risks.
- Navy Air’s current ITSM environment is fragmented and lacks standard SLAs, requiring significant operational upgrades for self-hosting.
- Ashish noted that on-premises hosting offers control but not necessarily risk reduction, warning of potential operational risks.
- The main cloud concern is aggregated CMDB data, which can create sensitive operational intelligence even from unclassified records.
- Ashish recommended a tiered CMDB, keeping sensitive details out of SaaS platforms, using field encryption, and exporting logs for monitoring.
- He advised creating a regulator evidence pack before hosting decisions, including data classification, encryption, access controls, and incident workflows.
- Cloud SaaS can be made defensible if framed as an aviation safety risk management case, not just a commercial procurement.
- HYOK (Hold Your Own Key) strengthens cloud security but is not sufficient alone; it must be part of layered controls and not justify storing classified data.
- ServiceNow Vault should be seen as a control accelerator, not a complete solution; poor data governance cannot be solved by Vault alone.
- Compensating controls should include contractual review, EU support commitments, break glass procedures, and customer-controlled encryption.
- Ashish warned against letting AI ambitions weaken initial security architecture, recommending selective encryption and AI zoning.
- He suggested classifying data into AI-eligible, AI-restricted, and AI-prohibited categories, prioritizing safety and regulatory compliance.
- Follow-up actions include sharing Gartner research notes and a written response, ensuring Navy Air receives tailored recommendations.

Specifically, how should a university or similarly complex, siloed organization approach the development, governance, and adoption of KM and digital tools to drive sustainable cultural change, staff empowerment, and measurable value?
Analyst Name: Francesco Vicchi
Discussion Summary: 1. Enterprise KM Roadmap: A Phased Approach
A successful transformation should follow clear, iterative milestones to move from a siloed state to an optimized, AI-enhanced ecosystem:
•	Phase 1: Assessment & Foundation 
o	Maturity Assessment: Evaluate current KM maturity across faculties. Knowledge Management Maturity Assessment: Evaluate Before Implementing AI 
o	Search Gap Analytics: Use semantic search tools to identify how often users search for topics that are currently not covered in your knowledge base.
o	Stakeholder Engagement: Identify "KM Champions" in academic and administrative units to ensure diverse representation and structure their knowledge the knowledge using AI tools.
•	Phase 2: Consolidation & Standardization 
o	Unified Platform: Continue integrating fragmented knowledge into a single enterprise platform (e.g., ServiceNow) to ensure interoperability.
o	Establish Content Standards: Implement a style guide based on the 10 Attributes for Effective KM Articles, focusing on titles, clarity, and structured formats.Quick Answer: How to Make Knowledge Management Articles AI-Ready 
•	Phase 3: Integration & Digital Enablement 
o	GenAI-Facilitated Capture: Use LLMs to summarize interaction transcripts (from Teams, Zoom, or chat) to turn "byproducts" of normal work into structured knowledge assets. Quick Answer: AI Use Cases for Managing Knowledge Content at Scale and How Generative AI Impacts Knowledge Management 
o	Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): Deploy RAG to allow GenAI to use your unique enterprise resources (like resolved tickets) as the basis for accurate, context-aware responses.
•	Phase 4: Adoption & Continuous Improvement 
o	Mindset Shift: Roll out change management that trains staff to curate content for machines as well as humans.
o	AI-Driven Health Management: Use analytics dashboards to flag duplicates, expiring content, or "knowledge gaps".
2. Breaking Down Silos: Cross-Departmental Collaboration
To foster a culture of sharing across academic and administrative units:
•	Dynamic Expertise Directories: Use GenAI to automatically profile staff expertise by analyzing documents and messages. This helps employees find and connect with "who knows what" across departmental boundaries.
•	Cross-Functional Working Groups: Establish KM groups with representatives from different faculties to set shared standards.
•	Incentive Programs: Recognize knowledge contributions through formal metrics and recognition to encourage a shift from "knowledge hoarding" to sharing. Eliminate Silos Now to Unlock Full AI ROI in Customer Service 
3. Governance: Frameworks for Effective KM
Robust governance prevents "knowledge chaos" as you scale AI-generated content:
•	Central Steering Committee: A central body should set strategy, while Departmental KM Leads manage local content and champion adoption.
•	Human-in-the-Loop Validation: All AI-generated or revised content must be reviewed by a human expert before publication to ensure accuracy and prevent hallucinations.
•	Robust Archival Methods: Establish strict archival processes. Unlike humans, GenAI chatbots will not automatically know to ignore outdated information, making a clean repository critical.
4. Cultural Change & Staff Empowerment
Scaling KM is as much a cultural challenge as a technical one:
•	Empowerment through Automation: Use GenAI to act as a "scribe," turning SME interviews or meeting transcripts into draft articles. This reduces the time burden on your experts.
•	Storytelling: Communicate value by sharing real-world impacts, such as how KM has reduced time-to-resolution for student requests.
•	Training for "Atomized Authoring": Train staff in modular content creation, where small "atoms" of text are created to be easily combined by AI for different contexts (e.g., chatbot answers vs. full articles).

•	Existing controls include baseline DLP (e.g., restrictions to mass media, email encryption) and detective DLP (detecting data exfiltration after the fact). The team is now focused on shifting to a more proactive, preventive approach.

Business Engagement and Best Practices
•	The team is engaging business units to define “what good looks like,” identify high-risk behaviors, and validate DLP use cases (e.g., whether a relationship manager exporting contacts to Gmail is acceptable).
•	Paulo strongly endorsed this stakeholder engagement as a best practice, emphasizing that DLP programs often fail when controls are implemented without business validation.
DLP Program: Building the Culture Through Business Collaboration and Governance

Evolving DLP: From Reactive to Contextual and Proactive
•	Traditional DLP is reactive and binary (block/allow) with little context or thresholds, often disrupting business workflows.
•	Modern solutions (like Cyberhaven) offer more context and intent analysis, including workflow analysis, pattern recognition, data lineage, and risk scoring. This enables more nuanced, risk-based controls and phased deployment.

Phased and Targeted Rollout
•	Both Paulo and Jessica highlighted the value of starting with monitor mode for specific high-risk actions or user groups, rather than enabling controls organization-wide, to avoid alert fatigue and performance issues.
•	Early feedback loops with pilot groups or high-risk departments are critical for tuning policies before broader rollout.

User Training, Communication, and Change Management
•	User awareness and training are essential to reduce resistance and clarify the purpose of DLP (i.e., protecting data, not monitoring employees).
•	Paulo recommended a hybrid approach: proactive communication (e.g., intranet updates, FAQs, policy templates) before rollout, and “just-in-time” notifications/pop-ups during enforcement.
•	Controls should not just block actions but guide users to approved alternatives (e.g., “If you need to share data, use this approved tool”).

Escalation Paths and Business Involvement
•	Current escalation involves legal, compliance, and HR, but not the business unit directly. Paulo recommended involving business representatives during investigations to validate scenarios, though with caution regarding potential conflicts of interest.
•	Clearly defined escalation paths and roles are critical for timely incident response.

Documentation and Auditability
•	All decisions, use cases, and policy changes should be documented for audit and continuous improvement. Paulo recommended a simple central repository (e.g., SharePoint, Confluence, ServiceNow) linked to change tickets, not just for compliance but to ensure business alignment.

Tool and Capability Gaps
•	The team identified gaps in Cyberhaven’s ability to enforce complex email logic (e.g., conditional rules in Outlook/O365). Paulo confirmed that Purview’s adaptive DLP is not yet mature for these scenarios.
•	He recommended considering additional tools such as Abnormal Security, Proofpoint, and Mimecasrtr, which are advancing in adaptive and AI-driven DLP for email.

Date: 25-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20137731
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: IT/Infrastructure and Operations - Other Role
Purpose: Area Office Infrastructure Standardization – Incident and DR Readiness Pack
Question Asked: kindly review the attached Incident and DR Readiness document and provide your written feedback and recommendations.

This document is intended to support Area Office incident readiness, DR readiness, compliance reporting, and reduction of Area Office related incidents under the Area Office Infrastructure Standardization objective.

Attachment:

1.	KUFPEC AO Incident DR Readiness Pack.docx — Pages 1–20 only
Due to the 20-page review limit, I am sharing pages 1–20 in this email. I can send the remaining pages separately if required.

Please confirm whether the attached content is sufficient from a best-practice perspective, or if any updates are required
Analyst Name: Wayne Hankins
Discussion Summary: I had a few suggestions and questions that could help further strengthen the document:
1.	Containment Authority Clarification
In the Roles & Responsibilities section, it would be helpful to explicitly clarify whether the AO IT Lead requires approval from the AO General Manager before executing containment actions (e.g., isolating systems). In most incident scenarios, especially P1/P2, speed is critical—so it would be good to clearly state what actions the AO IT Lead is empowered to take immediately versus those requiring business approval.
2.	End-User Incident Reporting
In Phase 1 (Identify and Declare), the plan references alerts from tools or “user reports,” but it doesn’t specify how end users should report incidents. Consider adding a short subsection defining the expected reporting channels (e.g., ServiceNow portal, email alias, hotline, Teams, etc.) to reduce ambiguity during real events.
3.	Playbooks / Runbooks
The containment section is strong, but it raises the question of whether these response steps are backed by detailed operational playbooks. If so, it would be useful to reference them explicitly (or link them). If not, developing playbooks for common scenarios (ransomware, account compromise, network breach) would significantly improve execution consistency.
4.	Secure Recovery Environment
In the recovery phase, it would be helpful to clarify whether restores are performed in an isolated/secure recovery environment before reintroduction to production. This is especially important for ransomware scenarios to avoid reinfection.
5.	Ransomware-Specific Reality vs. DR Targets
The RPO/RTO section is solid for traditional DR, but in real-world ransomware events, meeting these targets is often not immediately feasible. There are typically additional steps that fall outside normal DR, such as:
o	Stopping the attack
o	Forensics and evidence collection
o	Ransom/negotiation decisions
o	Securing and rebuilding foundational infrastructure
o	Validating/cleaning backups before use
o	Establishing a minimum viable environment before full restoration
It may be worth explicitly acknowledging this in the document or adding a ransomware-specific recovery overlay, so expectations are realistic.
6.	BIA Alignment and Recovery Sequencing
For the system inventory and recovery tiers, I’d recommend explicitly tying this to an up-to-date Business Impact Analysis (BIA). The BIA should drive both system prioritization and the sequence of recovery, rather than just static tier classification.
7.	Lastly, review this new note and see how you can incorporate it into your IR plan: Tool: Incident Response Checklist for Third-Party Cyber Incidents

Date: 9-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19432982
Buyer Region: JAPAN
Buyer Industry: Services
Buyer Role: Head of AI
Purpose: E7のサービス内容
Question Asked: 1・E7はこれまでとどのようなサービスが追加されているのか
　（エージェント開発やグローバルのガバナンスなどの機能は何処まで網羅されているのか）
2・現在、「E5 Security」と「E3」の組み合わせで契約しているが
　E7と比較して不足している点、追加されている点は何か
3・現在、2プラン契約しているようにE7と個別プランで契約することによるメリット・デメリットは？
Analyst Name: Koichiro Yumi
Discussion Summary: ME7の内容説明に加えて現行利用パターン（M365E3+E5 Security)との機能差を踏まえたメリット・デメリットについて言及しました。

1. Microsoft 365 E7で追加されるサービスとエージェント／ガバナンス機能網羅性
ME7の簡単な紹介と３つの機能について説明。2026年5月1日に提供開始される「Microsoft 365 E7（ME7）」は、1ユーザーあたり月額99ドルで提供される新バンドル。 
ME7は、「M365 E5」に「Microsoft 365 Copilot」「Agent 365」「Entra Suite」の3つを追加した構成となっている。

エージェント開発およびグローバルガバナンスについては、E7に含まれる「Agent 365」がその役割を担う。
	• 網羅されている機能: 
		○ Agent 365は、Microsoft環境におけるAIエージェントのコントロールプレーン（管理基盤）です。M365管理センターの一部として機能し、Copilot StudioやAI Foundryで開発されたカスタムエージェントに加え、SDKを統合したサードパーティ製エージェント（ServiceNowなど）も一元管理・検出（インベントリ化）できます。セキュリティやガバナンスは、既存のEntra（Agent IDの付与）、Purview（秘密度ラベルやDLP）、Defenderのシグナルを活用してポリシーを適用・制御する。
	• 不足している機能（発展途上な点）: 
		○ 現在のAgent 365は「ワーク・イン・プログレス（発展途上）」と評価されている。高度なライフサイクル管理や、ユーザーの代理ではなく完全に自律して動く「エージェンティック・ユーザー」向けのポリシー適用機能はまだ初期段階であり、機能ギャップが存在する。現状では、月額15ドル（E7に含まれる単価）のプレミアム価格を正当化するだけの新機能や専用機能は十分に備わっていない。
		
2. 現在の「E3 ＋ E5 Security」と「E7」の機能差（不足・追加点）
現在の「M365 E3 ＋ E5 Security」構成と比較して、E7で追加される機能（現在不足している機能）は以下の2つのカテゴリに分かれる。
 ① E5ベースで追加される機能:
	○ M365 E5 Compliance: Purview eDiscoveryやTeams DLPなどの高度なコンプライアンスおよび情報保護機能。
	○ Power BI Pro: 高度なビジネス分析ツール。
	○ Teams Phone Standard: クラウドベースの電話システム。
 ② E7固有で追加される機能:
	○ Microsoft 365 Copilot: 生成AIアシスタント機能。
	○ Agent 365: 上記1で解説したエージェント管理機能。
	○ Entra Suite: Private Access、Internet Access、ID Governanceなどの高度なゼロトラストネットワーク/ID管理機能。

3. E7（包括バンドル）と個別プラン（E3+アドオン等）のメリット・デメリットと交渉術
2027年2月の更改に向けて、ME7のような上位バンドルと、現状のような個別プランを併用する場合の比較および交渉術は以下の通り。
【個別プラン（E3 + 必要なアドオン）のメリット・デメリット】
• メリット（コスト最適化）: 
	○ 組織のニーズに合わせてライセンスを適正化（ライトサイジング）することで、全社一律で高機能バンドル（E5やE7）を導入するのと比較して、10%〜37%のコストを削減できる。
　　　不要な機能（Power BIや高度な電話機能など）に対する「シェルフウェア（使われないライセンス）」の無駄払いを防げる。
• デメリット（交渉力の低下）: 
	○ 複数のSKUを管理する運用の手間が増える。また、更新時にMicrosoftの戦略製品（E5やCopilotなど）を追加しない場合、「現状維持の更新」とみなされ、Microsoftから提示される
　　　　割引率が大幅に低下、あるいは定価での更新となるリスクが極めて高くなる。
		
【E7（包括プラン）のメリット・デメリット】
• メリット（強力な交渉レバレッジ）: 
	○ Microsoftは現在、E5、Copilot、および新設のE7の普及を最優先している。全社導入する必要はなく、エグゼクティブや特定の高度AI活用部門に限定して少数のE7を導入するだけで、
　　　契約全体のE3やアドオンに対する強力な割引を引き出すための「レバレッジ（交渉材料）」として機能する。
• デメリット（コストと制約）: 
	○ E7は月額99ドルと非常に高額。さらに、E7のバンドル割引率は13.2%であり、E3（14.5%）やE5（16.4%）と比較して上位バンドルであるにもかかわらず割引率が低く設定されている。
　　　また、オンプレミスからの移行優遇である「From SA（FSA）」SKUがE7には用意されないため、FSAの権利を維持したい場合は「E5 FSA」を購入した上でE7へのステップアップを購入
　　　するなどの複雑な対応が必要になる。

Analyst Name: Gilbert van der Heiden
Discussion Summary: Earlier this week Roma, you and me discussed IT4IT in the context of an enterprise information model.
I am attaching the AskGartner response to the questions you raised as input for the call.
On the call I learned that you already have quite some models in place, and Roma also referred to OCSF – which is a security framework that I am not familiar with.
When focusing on IT4IT I shared the framework characteristics for IT4IT 3.0.1 with the focus on data objects as the connecting tissue across the functional groups and value streams (page 46, 47).
In that context I mentioned that IT4IT similar to Servicenow’s CSDM uses the Digital Product as the leading object.

On the call you mentioned you have Servicenow, and in that case, it would be good to consider the CSDM 5 framework, as it comes with wider details that Roma can build on. On the call I showed the model on page 17/18 that explains the breakdown of a product into components, which is what supports the practical application of your intended information model

In operationalizing, I asked if you use an EA tool and you mentioned you are implementing Ardoq. I mentioned that Ardoq applies its own metamodel and in that respect, here is link to their approach to metamodels – I picked the link to the autogenerated metamodel as that is the most commonly applied approach to create a metamodel in Ardoq: https://help.ardoq.com/en/articles/44060-autogenerated-metamodel

Considering the potential complexity, my suggestion was to focus on the level of detail you need to make strategic or at best tactical decisions.
Trying to implement any framework at detail across multiple systems and tools becomes virtually impossible to manage or even maintain.

With that in mind, using Ardoq is a good idea, but I would still suggest to start with the 8 Steps to Select and Obtain Value From Enterprise Architecture Tools. At least read the first couple of steps to make sure you implement what you need, not everything that might be possible.

In terms of further research, do look at the AskGartner response and in addition, consider:
•	Ontologies Are Crucial to Improve AI Accuracy and Reduce Costs 
•	CSDM5 reference in: Save Your Failing CMDB With a Service Data Model 
•	IT4IT reference in: The Essential Delivery Models and IT Tools for Platform-Centric I&O

o	Eligibility screening: AI can analyze applicant information to assess eligibility, which can free up grant managers for more complex reviews. 
o	Predictive analytics: AI can analyze historical data to predict the success of new proposals and guide funding decisions. 
o	Risk assessment: AI can identify potential risks associated with applicants, which can help with resource allocation. 
o	Application reviews: AI can automate application reviews and flag high-potential submissions. 
o	Grant writing: AI can help with the creation, editing, and submission of grant proposals. 
o	Training: AI can train grant management staff to enhance workflow efficiency.

Target Personas: CIOs, Heads of I&O/ITSM, SRE & Cloud Ops leaders, Problem Managers, and Business Operations heads across key verticals.

Questions/Feedback Requested:
- Whether the category positioning (Ticketless IT vs. traditional AIOps/ITSM) is clear and compelling?
- Strength and differentiation of the value narrative?
- How well the messaging aligns with current IT operations trends and enterprise readiness?
- Any gaps that would strengthen the story for broader market impact?
Analyst Name: Colin Fletcher
Discussion Summary: Key ask:
To refine the company's positioning and messaging to clearly articulate differentiated value for both enterprise buyers and individual IT stakeholders in the autonomous IT and ticketless space.

Summary:
- The discussion focused on feedback Colin Fletcher provided regarding the team's blog post and positioning around "ticketless" IT operations.
- VS Joshi raised concerns about the term "ticketless," questioning its market traction and the effort required to evangelize it.
- Colin clarified that "ticketless" is not widely used by buyers and is seen as an enterprise value, not an individual value.
- Colin emphasized the need to connect the platform’s value to individual career growth, especially for ITSM platform champions.
- He advised that messaging should address both organizational ambitions and individual fears about AI’s impact on IT roles.
- Colin recommended highlighting how human contributions and tacit knowledge are leveraged and recognized within the platform.
- He suggested amplifying case studies that show how freed-up time enables higher-value work for IT teams.
- Varun Sharma asked for feedback on the deck’s framing, seeking to ensure it resonates with enterprise buyers.
- Colin advised focusing messaging on incremental adoption and clear, specific use cases rather than broad platform claims.
- He stressed the importance of anchoring differentiation on one core attribute—such as speed, confidence, or cost—rather than claiming all.
- Colin noted that many differentiators listed, like predictive prevention and explainable AI, are common in the market and need sharper proof points.
- He recommended using concrete metrics, proof of value, and examples of sustainable innovation to substantiate claims.
- The team discussed positioning as an "agentic AI company for autonomous IT," but Colin noted this is not yet distinctive in a crowded market.
- Colin concluded with tactical advice: start small, refine the "ticketless" concept with a unique angle, and study the digital employee experience market for aspirational positioning.
